record.paper_title: Open Problems in the Function Theory of the Bergman Space
record.original_question: Let A be a zero sequence for L2_a(D), let G_A be its associated zero divisor, and let I(A) = {f in L2_a(D): f vanishes on A}. Does G_A generate I(A) as an invariant subspace, meaning that the functions G_A, zG_A, z^2G_A, and so on span a dense subspace of I(A)?

evidence.quote: Problem 4.1. Does G_A generate I(A) = {f ∈ L2_a(D) : f = 0 on A} as an invariant subspace? In other words, do the functions G_A, zG_A, z2G_A, ... span a dense subspace of I(A)?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disk, and let
$$L^2_a(\mathbb{D})=\Big\{f\text{ holomorphic on }\mathbb{D}:\|f\|^2=\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f(z)|^2\,dA(z)<\infty\Big\}$$
be the Bergman space, where $dA$ is normalized area measure. A sequence $A=\{a_n\}\subset\mathbb{D}$ (with multiplicities) is called a zero sequence for $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ if there exists a nonzero $f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ whose zero set (counted with multiplicity) contains $A$. For such a zero sequence, define
$$I(A)=\{f\in L^2_a(\mathbb{D}): f \text{ vanishes on } A\text{ (with multiplicity)}\},$$
which is a closed $M_z$-invariant subspace of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ (here $M_z$ denotes multiplication by the coordinate function $z$). The associated canonical zero divisor $G_A\in I(A)$ is the unique solution of the extremal problem
$$G_A(0)=\sup\{\operatorname{Re} f(0): f\in I(A),\ \|f\|\le 1\},$$
normalized so that $G_A(0)>0$.

Question: Does $G_A$ generate $I(A)$ as an $M_z$-invariant subspace? Equivalently, is the linear span of $\{G_A, zG_A, z^2 G_A, z^3 G_A,\dots\}$ dense in $I(A)$?
artifact.status_search_result: The question was answered affirmatively by Aleman, Richter, and Sundberg in "Beurling's Theorem for the Bergman space" (Acta Math. 177 (1996), 275–310). Their result implies that every invariant subspace M of $L^2_a(\mathbb{D})$ equals the closure of the span of $\{z^n(M\ominus zM):n\ge 0\}$. For a zero-based invariant subspace $I(A)$, the wandering subspace $I(A)\ominus zI(A)$ is one-dimensional and spanned by the canonical divisor $G_A$, so $G_A$ generates $I(A)$.

status_evidence.title: Beurling's Theorem for the Bergman space
status_evidence.snippet: Every invariant subspace M of A^2(D) equals [M ⊖ zM], the smallest invariant subspace containing the wandering subspace.
status_evidence.claim: Aleman, Richter, and Sundberg proved a Beurling-type theorem that implies the canonical zero divisor generates the zero-based invariant subspace.

status_evidence.title: Recent Progress and Open Problems in the Bergman Space
status_evidence.snippet: The canonical divisor of any A^p zero-set generates the corresponding invariant subspace N^p.
status_evidence.claim: It is reported as known that the canonical divisor generates the zero-based invariant subspace.
